<reason>PRO built a tight, physically grounded case (threshold accumulation, tests as the only purely optional fragmentation source, catalog-based verifiability, narrow scope) and then forced CON onto the defensive with two well-aimed pressure questions. CON's answers were damaging to its own position: it conceded the "benefit" of a test is a credential that "does not have to outweigh" a 2007-style cloud, and admitted that "none" of its preferred alternatives stop a deliberate smash either. That left CON's central move—demanding the treaty "prevent" cascades by reaching war and mass—looking like a standard no instrument meets, and PRO correctly noted CON's disposal/traffic rules are compatible rather than competing. CON's relabeling and "untrusted weapon fired more" lines were plausibly answered (fragments are the evidence; planners don't build around unvalidated systems). CON's closing rhetoric ("changing the photo, not the physics") was sharp, but the underlying weighing had already been undercut. PRO's repeated clipping was a real execution cost and keeps the margin from being larger.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure-question follow-through: after asking CON to name the concrete benefit of the next test and why the wartime hole is fatal only for the treaty, CON answered with a credential that "does not have to outweigh" the debris and admitted its own rules stop "none" of the deliberate smashes; PRO's closing turned both admissions into the decisive weighing—permanent fragments against nothing worth keeping.</best_rebuttal>
